qa.question:
Would the board and management provide greater clarity on the following operational 
and financial matters? Specifically:  
 
(i) 
Single-Scan Serialization (3S): The group has spent several years seeking retail 
industry adoption of its 3S solutions, including the commercialising of RFID-
enabled 3S solutions over the past two years. Sales of 3S barcodes increased by 
$238,000, or 45.2%, from $526,000 in FY2025 to $764,000 in FY2026. Did the 3S 
business achieve operating break-even in FY2026 and what evidence 
supports the view that the loss prevention business is approaching a 
material acceleration in adoption, rather than continuing to experience 
gradual growth? If not, how much more investment is needed to get the 
group to that point and what revenue, margin and customer adoption 
milestones must be achieved to justify that investment?  
 
(ii) 
Healthcare (Automated Visual Acuity Test Device (AVAT)): Could 
management explain the intended business and revenue model? The group 
has deployed AVAT devices at three sites in Singapore. How do the current 
deployment numbers, utilisation rates and revenue compare with the 
original business case, and what milestones must be achieved for AVAT to 
become commercially viable? 
 
(iii) 
Healthcare (AI-driven osteoarthritis detection): What unmet clinical need 
does the proposed solution address, and how has the group validated 
demand among its intended users and paying customers? Given the group’s 
existing capabilities, market access and financial strength, what 
competitive advantage qualifies it to enter this field, and does it have the 
clinical partnerships, distribution channels and primary-care network 
needed to commercialise the solution at scale? What is the estimated size of 
the addressable market?

The group recorded a loss before tax of $(3.12) million in FY2026. As seen from the 
consolidated statement of profit or loss, the group’s gross profit and rental income (under 
other operating income) were insufficient to cover administrative and other operating 
expenses.  
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
(i) 
Given the group’s continued losses, will the board conduct a strategic review 
of the long-term viability of Sakae Sushi and Hei Sushi, including their 
relevance to local consumers, competitive positioning and ability to 
generate sustainable returns after corporate overheads are included? 
 
Despite its reported losses, the group continued to broaden and diversify its food-related 
businesses and acquired Cooking Art Industries Pte. Ltd. (Cooking Art) which specialises in 
the supply and distribution of Nonya kuehs and pastries. 
 
(ii) 
Can management explain the strategic rationale for acquiring a business 
specialising in Nonya kuehs and pastries, given the group’s existing focus on 
sushi restaurants? What specific synergies does it expect between the two 
businesses, and how will these be realised and measured?  

The aggregate consideration for Cooking Art was $741,000, and the transaction was 
completed on 2 April 2026. According to the purchase price allocation in Note 12(b) on page 
75, Cooking Art had total identifiable net liabilities of $(134,000). As a result, goodwill of 
$875,000 was recognised in the financial statements.  
 
(iii) 
What due diligence and valuation methodology did the board rely on to 
approve the acquisition? In particular, what earnings and cash flow 
forecasts supported the purchase price, what investment hurdle rate and 
payback period were applied, and how were the expected synergies 
quantified?  
 
(iv) 
What competitive advantages does Cooking Art possess in its market, 
particularly in product quality, brand recognition, distribution reach, 
customer relationships and pricing power? Following the acquisition, will it 
retain independent management and operating autonomy, or be integrated 
into the group’s existing operations?

Note 9 (Property, plant and equipment; page 67) shows a $3.9 million addition to 
leasehold land during the year. According to Note 26 (Segment information; page 95), this 
has been attributed to the “Sakae Sushi” operating segment.  
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
(i) 
Could management clarify the nature of this $3.9 million addition to 
leasehold land? Does it relate to the acquisition of a property, an additional 
leasehold interest or another transaction?  
 
(ii) 
What is the intended use of this addition and what specific operational or 
strategic need does this addition address?

capitalisation of around S$10 million.

Despite the broader strength of the Singapore equity market, the company’s share price has 
remained largely stagnant over the past several years. The group has also incurred 
substantial losses attributable to shareholders over the past three financial years  
 
FY2026 – $(2.81) million 
FY2025 – $(4.03) million 
FY2024 – $(3.03) million 
 
The group’s accumulated losses increased from $(8.4) million as at 1 January 2016 to $(39.8)

liabilities, what amount could potentially be returned to shareholders, and 
how does this compare with the value implied by the current market 
capitalisation?  
 
If the board believes continuing operations would deliver greater value to 
shareholders, 
especially 
minority 
shareholders, 
what 
quantified 
assumptions support that conclusion?

qa.question:
As disclosed in the annual report by both the chairman and CEO, management has set a 
target to double revenue by FY2031, while maintaining gross profit margin above 50% and 
keeping overhead costs below 20% of revenue. 
 
(i) 
What revenue contribution does management expect from the group’s core 
back-end consumable tooling business versus its high-precision build-to-
print component manufacturing business serving front-end wafer fab 
equipment (WFE) in order to achieve the FY2031 revenue target? What are 
the key assumptions for growth in each segment? 
 
(ii) 
Given the cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry and the significant 
investment associated with AI infrastructure, what assumptions does 
management make about semiconductor demand and the WFE cycle 
through FY2031? Does the board see any significant risk of the industry 
entering a downcycle in the near term, and how would this affect the group’s 
growth and investment plans? 
 
(iii) 
To what extent does the group’s FY2031 growth plan depend on 
acquisitions, particularly in the WFE segment? What capabilities, 
technologies or geographic markets, if any, would management seek to 
acquire?

The company will report a new segment, “Build-to-print Precision Components”, 
starting in FY2027.  
 
(Source: company annual report) 

Until FY2024, the group reported its segments on a geographical basis. Following a change 
in its internal reporting for decision-making and performance analysis, the group revised its 
reportable segments in accordance with SFRS(I) 8, Operating Segments. In FY2025 and 
FY2026, the group has reported three segments: Consumable Tools, WFE Parts, and 
Corporate and Others. 
 
(i) 
Can the board or audit & risk Committee (ARC) help shareholders better 
understand whether the new “Build-to-print Precision Components” 
segment is principally a reclassification of the existing WFE Parts business, 
or whether it represents an expansion or reorganisation of the business? 
What has changed in the underlying activities, customer base, capabilities, 
strategic positioning or management structure? 
 
(ii) 
How much of the group’s core capabilities in consumable tooling are 
transferable to the manufacture of precision components for WFE, and what 
additional manufacturing capabilities, processes, technology or expertise 
does the group need to develop to compete effectively in this market? 
 
While the group did not report any customer contributing more than 10% of total group’s 
revenue this year, it identified a major customer in the WFE segment contributing 
approximately $6.2 million to $6.3 million in revenue in each of the past two financial years.  
 
(iii) 
Can management help shareholders understand where MMUS sits in the 
WFE supply chain today, including whether it supplies directly to OEMs, 
contract manufacturers or other Tier 1 suppliers? Is MMUS itself qualified 
as a Tier 1 supplier to any major WFE customers, and how does the group 
intend to leverage its current position to identify, qualify for and win more 
large WFE customers?

Total capital expenditure for FY2026 amounted to $3.8 million, of which $3.0 million 
was for plant and equipment, with the majority relating to the WFE segment.  
 
The CEO has disclosed that the group expects to invest $12.0 million in FY2027 to support 
its five-year plan, including expanding operations in markets where the group’s customers 
are growing and investing in next-generation processes and smarter manufacturing. 
 
This represents a significant increase in capital expenditure compared with $1.2 million in 
FY2025 and $2.0 million in FY2024. 
 
(i) 
Can management provide a breakdown of the planned $12.0 million of 
FY2027 capital expenditure between the consumable tools and WFE 
businesses? 
 
(ii) 
How much of the planned FY2027 capital expenditure is already supported 
by committed customer orders, contracts or capacity requirements, and 
how much is intended to build capacity ahead of anticipated demand?  

The group reported an earnings per share of 11.44 cents for FY2026 and paid a dividend of

confidence that the higher investment programme will not come at the

qa.question:
Revenue for the past two years was supported by the sale of boutique development 
properties in Singapore, amounting to US$10.39 million in FY2026 and US$11.83 million in 
FY2025. The land for Paulownia at 25 Jalan Selanting was acquired in July 2022, with all 
units sold by FY2025. The land for Neoco at 15 Lynwood Grove was acquired in December 
2023, with one unit settled in FY2026 and the remaining two units sold but yet to be settled 
as at the end of the financial period. 
 
(i) 
Project returns and capital efficiency: What return on invested capital did 
each project generate or is expected to generate? Over the development 
cycle, do these calculations fully capture financing costs, corporate 
overheads, professional fees and other costs attributable to the project? For 
instance, employee benefits expense for the year was relatively high at US$5.8 
million, while the share of results of associates and joint ventures was US$9.7 
million, compared with profit before tax of US$5.6 million, which raises questions 
about the overall profitability and capital efficiency of the group.  
 
(ii) 
Growth: Can management elaborate on the group’s growth strategy beyond 
boutique landed developments in Singapore? 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
The five-year highlights are set out on page 19 of the annual report. Over this period, net 
asset value per share has increased modestly, while shareholders’ equity has declined, partly 
reflecting cumulative dividends and share buybacks. The group generated an average return 
on equity of approximately 2% over the period, while more than US$9.1 million was spent 
on share buybacks. 

(Adapted from company annual report) 
 
(iii) 
Has the board undertaken a formal assessment of whether its overall 
strategy has generated an adequate return on shareholders’ capital? In 
particular, how did the board determine that deploying more than US$9.1 
million on share buybacks represented an appropriate use of capital, 
relative to other available investment opportunities?

In 2023, the group diversified into student accommodation through the acquisition of a 
51% stake in Homestead Capital Pte. Ltd., which operates student accommodation 
properties under the “The Keystone” brand.  The total consideration was $5.3 million when 
the pre-money net tangible asset value of the target was just $388,528. As disclosed in the 
2024 annual report, intangible assets with a carrying value of US$4.16 million were 
recognised due to the acquisition, and an impairment of US$623,000 was already recognised 
in FY2024. 

In FY2026, following losses recorded by Homestead due to actual performance being lower 
than expectation amid competitive business environment, management has reassessed the 
recoverable amount of the CGU as at 30 June 2026 to be US$Nil. Within three years of 
acquisition, the full amount of intangible assets arising from the Homestead acquisition has 
been fully impaired.    
 
(i) 
Can the board help shareholders understand the original investment thesis 
for entering student accommodation in 2023? What were the key 
assumptions underpinning the investment case at the time, including 
expected occupancy, rental rates, operating margins, competitive 
positioning and returns, and what due diligence did the board undertake to 
validate those assumptions before committing capital? 
 
(ii) 
What did the board believe gave Homestead a sustainable competitive 
advantage when the investment was approved? 
 
(iii) 
What are the current plans for Homestead, and does the board intend to 
commit further capital to it? If so, what specific financial or operating 
milestones would Homestead be required to achieve before any further 
capital commitment is approved? 
 
(iv) 
Given the group’s past investments in Pacific Star Development, Envy Asset 
Management, and Homestead, can the board explain what specific changes 
have been made to the investment approval and oversight process? How has 
management accountability been addressed in light of these outcomes? 
What weighting, if any, do investment outcomes and capital allocation 
decisions carry within the executive remuneration framework?

Appointment of Mr Saw Meng Tee: The director was appointed as an

90b948f69c41c0cfa8d0f66b8dc6b145) 
 
Can the board disclose the formal search and nomination process
